claims.text: High-throughput composition screening combined with CALPHAD modeling and experimental validation can efficiently accelerate high-entropy-alloy discovery.

The combined DSC, in-situ diffraction, and CALPHAD approach can determine melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across multi-principal-element alloys.
The proposed properties can be determined with roughly 5% error.
The approach is applicable to multi-principal-element alloys at temperatures up to about 2000 K.
The relevant starting materials are typically as-cast, equiatomic or near-equiatomic 3–5-element alloys synthesized by arc melting or casting under inert gas or vacuum.
DSC heat-flow measurements determine the enthalpy of fusion.
The entropy of fusion can be obtained from the measured enthalpy of fusion and melting temperature using their ratio.
Diffraction can identify alloy phase composition and crystal structure.
In-situ diffraction can track phase fractions, lattice parameters, and transient phase transformations during heating.
In-situ diffraction can accurately capture volume change across melting.
Experimentally observed transformations and phase behavior can be used to improve the accuracy of a thermodynamic database.
CALPHAD models can combine experimental and theoretical thermodynamic information to describe solid and liquid phases over broad composition and temperature ranges.
CALPHAD-based screening can evaluate thousands of candidate high-entropy-alloy compositions.
The integrated method will produce reliable temperature-dependent values of Tm, ΔH, ΔS, ΔV, and liquid-phase behavior with about 5% accuracy.
Conventional measurements on selected compositions often have uncertainties exceeding 10%.
Predictive performance may degrade when robust thermodynamic datasets are unavailable or CALPHAD is extrapolated beyond validated composition and temperature ranges.
Extreme compositions, very high temperatures, solid-state transformations, and short-range order can increase errors in DSC and diffraction analyses.
Independent standardized measurements across multiple compositions and replicates can validate the integrated approach.
Persistent discrepancies greater than about 5% in melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, or volume change would falsify the stated accuracy claim.
Liquid-phase stability can be established through phase-fraction evolution.
